metadata.title: Jailbreak Bottom Position | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master the Jailbreak escape from bottom half guard. Technical guide covering setup, execution, and transitions. Advanced escape with 60% success rate when executed properly.

overview:
The Jailbreak is an advanced escape position from bottom half guard, most notably developed and popularized within the 10th Planet Jiu-Jitsu system. This dynamic position involves the bottom player creating an underhook while simultaneously inverting and rolling toward their back to create separation and escape the top player's pressure. The Jailbreak represents a critical escape option when traditional half guard retention becomes compromised, particularly against skilled passers who have established strong crossface and underhook control.

The position's effectiveness lies in its ability to transform defensive disadvantage into offensive opportunity through explosive movement and technical precision. By inverting and rolling through, the bottom player can escape to turtle, re-establish guard, or even take the back. The Jailbreak requires excellent timing, flexibility, and spatial awareness, as the escape window is brief and the consequences of mistiming can result in being flattened or passed completely. This technique has become increasingly important in modern no-gi competition, where traditional half guard frames are more easily defeated due to the absence of gi grips.
state_invariants: Bottom player maintains underhook on the same side as their trapped leg, with elbow tight to their own hip to prevent top player from flattening pressure
Bottom player's hips are turned toward their trapped leg side, creating space and angle necessary for the inverting roll motion
Bottom player's free leg (non-trapped leg) is actively posting or creating frames to prevent being flattened completely to the mat
Top player has established position in top half guard with crossface or overhook control, creating the pressure that necessitates the jailbreak escape
Bottom player's head and shoulders are actively inverting toward the mat as they initiate the rolling motion, using momentum to create separation from top pressure
prerequisites: Bottom player is in bottom half guard with top player establishing dominant pressure
Bottom player has secured underhook on the same side as trapped leg
Top player has compromised traditional half guard retention through crossface, overhook, or heavy shoulder pressure
Bottom player has sufficient space to begin inverting motion without being completely flattened
Bottom player possesses adequate flexibility and body awareness for inverted rolling movements
key_principles: Maintain underhook throughout the entire escape sequence to prevent top player from re-establishing control
Generate explosive momentum through hip movement and inversion to overcome top player's base and pressure
Time the escape when top player commits weight forward, making their base more vulnerable to being rolled through
Keep chin tucked and shoulders rounded during inversion to protect neck and enable smooth rolling motion
Use free leg actively to push off mat and create additional momentum for the inverting escape

counter_transitions.trigger: When top player drives chest forward to flatten, use their forward momentum to accelerate the roll
When top player bases out wide to prevent roll, dive under their hips to deep half guard
When top player follows the jailbreak roll, continue rolling motion through to re-guard

decision_tree.condition: If top player has heavy crossface pressure and is driving forward
If top player bases out wide to prevent roll and underhook remains secure
If top player follows the jailbreak roll motion
If underhook is lost during escape attempt

common_errors.error: Attempting jailbreak without securing underhook first
common_errors.consequence: Top player easily follows and establishes mount or side control during the roll
common_errors.correction: Always establish and maintain tight underhook with elbow connected to hip before initiating inversion

common_errors.error: Rolling too slowly without explosive momentum
common_errors.consequence: Top player has time to base out, flatten you, or follow the roll to maintain control
common_errors.correction: Generate explosive hip movement and commit fully to the roll once initiated - hesitation kills the escape

common_errors.error: Failing to tuck chin during inversion
common_errors.consequence: Risk of neck injury and inability to complete smooth rolling motion
common_errors.correction: Keep chin tucked to chest throughout entire escape, looking at your own belt to protect neck

common_errors.error: Not using free leg to push off mat
common_errors.consequence: Insufficient momentum to complete the roll, getting stuck mid-escape
common_errors.correction: Actively push with free leg to generate additional power and speed for the inverting motion

common_errors.consequence: Top player regains control immediately after escape attempt, often ending in worse position
common_errors.correction: Maintain death grip on underhook throughout entire sequence - this is your lifeline to safety

common_errors.consequence: Top player anticipates and counters by driving weight forward or stripping underhook
common_errors.correction: Set up the jailbreak with other attacks or movements, then execute explosively when top player commits weight

training_drills.name: Jailbreak Repetition Drill
training_drills.description: Partner holds bottom half guard with underhook, applies moderate crossface pressure. Bottom player executes jailbreak roll to turtle repeatedly, focusing on speed and technique. 10 reps per side, alternating.

training_drills.name: Jailbreak Timing Drill
training_drills.description: Top player alternates between driving forward pressure and basing wide. Bottom player reads pressure and executes jailbreak only when top player commits weight forward. Develops timing and pressure sensitivity.

training_drills.name: Progressive Resistance Jailbreak
training_drills.description: Start with compliant partner allowing jailbreak escape. Gradually increase resistance over 3 rounds: 30% resistance, 60% resistance, 90% resistance. Focus on maintaining technique under increasing pressure.

training_drills.name: Jailbreak to Back Take Chain
training_drills.description: Bottom player executes jailbreak while top player intentionally follows the roll. Bottom player practices continuing the momentum to take top player's back. Emphasizes capitalizing on common counter.

expert_insights.danaher: The jailbreak represents a critical understanding of how momentum and leverage can overcome positional disadvantage. The biomechanical principle at work here involves converting linear pressure from the top player into rotational escape through inverting motion. The underhook serves as the fulcrum point around which the entire escape rotates - lose this connection and the mechanical advantage disappears entirely. What makes this escape particularly effective is the way it exploits the top player's commitment to forward pressure. When they drive their chest and shoulder into you, attempting to flatten and control, their center of gravity moves forward and their base becomes vulnerable. The explosive inversion transforms their pressure into momentum for your escape. However, this requires precise timing - too early and they can adjust their base, too late and you're already flattened. The practitioner must develop the sensitivity to feel when the top player commits their weight point of no return, then execute the escape with full commitment and speed.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, the jailbreak is one of the highest-percentage escapes from bottom half guard when you're getting smashed by a skilled passer. I've used this countless times when guys are heavy on the crossface and I need to create immediate separation. The key thing people miss is that you can't be tentative with this - you have to fully commit to the roll or you end up in worse position. When I feel the crossface getting heavy and my other frames are collapsing, I secure that underhook like my life depends on it, because it does. Then I explode into the roll, using my free leg to push off hard. Most of the time I end up in turtle, which gives me way more options than staying flattened in half guard. Against really good guys who follow the roll, I've taken the back multiple times by continuing the momentum. The jailbreak is also a great way to surprise opponents - they think they're crushing you in half guard, then suddenly you're inverting and they're scrambling to keep up. It's become essential in my game for those situations where traditional half guard retention just isn't working.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: The jailbreak is one of the core escapes in the 10th Planet system, and it's saved my students in countless situations. What I love about this technique is how it completely changes the dynamic of the half guard battle. Most people think of half guard as this slow, grinding position, but the jailbreak is explosive and dynamic. When you're locked down and the guy on top is smashing you, the jailbreak gives you this burst escape option that can completely flip the script. The cool thing is how it chains with the rest of the lockdown system - if they defend the electric chair or the old school sweep, boom, hit the jailbreak. If they're ready for the jailbreak, you can use that underhook for other attacks. It's all about creating dilemmas for the top player. One thing I always stress is the importance of flexibility for this move. If you're tight in the hips and can't invert smoothly, the jailbreak becomes way harder. That's why we do so much warmup work on inverting and rolling movements in 10th Planet. Get comfortable being upside down and this escape becomes second nature. And when you really master it, you can hit the jailbreak and immediately transition to taking the back or re-establishing guard - it becomes this beautiful flow rather than just a defensive escape.

metadata.title: Jailbreak Position | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master the Jailbreak position escape from side control in BJJ. Dynamic re-guard system with 45-60% success rate. Learn the hip escape, frame creation, and guard recovery sequence.

overview:
The Jailbreak position represents a critical transitional state during the escape sequence from side control bottom. This dynamic position occurs when the bottom player successfully creates space through proper framing and hip movement, but has not yet fully recovered guard. The name 'Jailbreak' reflects the explosive nature of breaking free from the controlling pressure of side control.

This position is characterized by the bottom player creating sufficient space to insert their knee shield or establish frames while simultaneously preventing the top player from re-establishing dominant control. The Jailbreak is not a static position to be held, but rather a fleeting moment of opportunity that must be capitalized upon immediately. Success requires proper timing, explosive hip movement, and decisive commitment to the escape.

Mastering the Jailbreak position is essential for developing a comprehensive defensive game. It represents the bridge between being pinned under side control and achieving the safety of guard. The position demands both technical precision in frame placement and athletic commitment to the escape movement, making it a fundamental skill for practitioners at all levels.
state_invariants: Bottom player's inside shoulder has created space from the mat through bridging or hip escape, with the spine no longer completely flat against the ground
At least one frame is established with the forearm or hand creating distance against opponent's shoulder, neck, or hip to prevent immediate recapture
Bottom player's hips are mobile and not fully controlled by top player's weight, allowing for continued shrimping or guard recovery movements
Top player maintains some degree of chest-to-chest pressure but lacks the complete shoulder pin characteristic of tight side control
Bottom player's legs are active and working to establish hooks, knee shields, or create additional space rather than remaining flat and controlled
prerequisites: Currently defending from side control bottom position with opponent applying pressure
Successful creation of initial space through hip escape or bridge movement
Establishment of at least one defensive frame to maintain separation
Recognition of timing window when opponent's weight shifts or base is compromised
Sufficient energy reserves to execute explosive escape movement
key_principles: Maintain constant frame pressure to prevent opponent from closing distance and re-establishing tight side control
Keep hips mobile and continue shrimping movements to create progressive space for guard recovery
Protect the back by keeping shoulders squared to opponent and preventing them from taking your back during escape
Use explosive hip movement to insert knee shield or recover full guard before opponent can adjust their base
Chain multiple escape attempts together as opponent's weight and pressure constantly shift
Never remain static in this position - either advance to guard recovery or prepare for next escape cycle
Coordinate upper body frames with lower body movement to maximize space creation

counter_transitions.trigger: Opponent attempts to drive weight forward to recapture side control
Opponent commits weight to one side allowing rotation underneath
Opponent's base is elevated or they attempt to transition to mount
Opponent posts hand to prevent initial escape creating space for full recovery

decision_tree.condition: If opponent drives forward with heavy crossface pressure attempting to recapture side control
If opponent elevates their hips or attempts to transition to mount creating space
If opponent shifts weight to prevent guard recovery but exposes their back
If opponent maintains moderate pressure without committing to specific pass or recapture

common_errors.error: Pausing or resting in the Jailbreak position instead of immediately continuing the escape sequence
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent time to adjust their weight and base, recapturing tight side control and negating all escape progress
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant movement and chain multiple escape attempts together, treating Jailbreak as a transitional moment rather than a position to hold

common_errors.error: Dropping the defensive frame once initial space is created
common_errors.consequence: Opponent immediately drives forward and recaptures side control with crossface, crushing the escape attempt
common_errors.correction: Maintain rigid frames throughout the entire escape sequence until guard is fully recovered and frames can be replaced with guard retention grips

common_errors.error: Turning away from opponent and exposing the back during the escape
common_errors.consequence: Opponent takes the back or establishes turtle top position, advancing to a more dominant position than side control
common_errors.correction: Keep shoulders square to opponent throughout escape, using hip movement to create space while maintaining upper body alignment to protect the back

common_errors.error: Using only upper body strength to push opponent away without coordinating hip movement
common_errors.consequence: Arms fatigue quickly while opponent simply waits out the pushing effort before re-establishing pressure with minimal effort
common_errors.correction: Coordinate frames with explosive hip escapes and shrimps, using frames to create and maintain space while hips do the work of recovery

common_errors.error: Attempting to recover full closed guard immediately from Jailbreak against a heavy opponent
common_errors.consequence: Opponent smashes through the incomplete guard recovery, passing directly to mount or knee on belly
common_errors.correction: Accept incremental progress by first recovering to knee shield, half guard, or butterfly guard before working to close the guard fully

common_errors.error: Keeping legs extended and static instead of actively working them to establish hooks or shields
common_errors.consequence: Opponent easily controls the hips and prevents any meaningful guard recovery despite successful upper body escape
common_errors.correction: Immediately begin establishing butterfly hooks, knee shields, or De La Riva hooks as soon as space is created, using active leg movement to secure guard

training_drills.name: Jailbreak Flow Drill
training_drills.description: Partner applies moderate side control pressure. Bottom player creates space through hip escape, establishes frames, and flows through multiple guard recovery options (half guard, closed guard, butterfly) in succession. Partner maintains light resistance to allow technique repetition. Focus on smooth transitions and constant movement.

training_drills.name: Timed Escape Drill
training_drills.description: Bottom player starts under tight side control and must escape to any form of guard within 30 seconds. Partner applies progressive resistance from 50% initially to 80% as student improves. Track success rate and identify which escape sequences work best under pressure. Builds urgency and explosive movement.

training_drills.name: Frame Maintenance Challenge
training_drills.description: From Jailbreak position with space already created, bottom player must maintain frames and prevent side control recapture while partner attempts to close distance for 60 seconds. Emphasizes frame endurance, hip mobility, and defensive awareness. Bottom player loses if opponent recaptures tight side control.

training_drills.name: Chain Escape Sequences
training_drills.description: Bottom player attempts primary escape (hip escape to half guard). If partner successfully defends, immediately chain to secondary option (technical stand-up or deep half entry). Continue chaining different escapes until successful guard recovery. Develops adaptability and multiple escape pathways.

expert_insights.danaher: The Jailbreak position represents a critical junction point in the escape hierarchy where mechanical advantage shifts from the top player to the bottom player, but only if the bottom player recognizes and exploits this window immediately. The biomechanical principle at work is the creation of structural frames that redirect the opponent's pressure away from your center of mass while simultaneously creating the angular space necessary for hip escape. The common failure mode is treating this as a position to hold rather than a transitional opportunity to exploit. The frame must be maintained with skeletal structure rather than muscular effort, allowing the larger muscle groups of the hips and legs to generate the explosive movement necessary for guard recovery. This position demands both technical precision in frame placement and athletic commitment to the escape sequence.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, the Jailbreak is where matches are won or lost on the bottom. If you can't capitalize on this moment when you've created space, you'll spend the entire match getting crushed under side control. I focus on making the Jailbreak as brief as possible - the moment I create that space with my frame, I'm exploding my hips and recovering to half guard or standing up. The key is having multiple options ready because your opponent is also trying to recapture, so if they shut down your hip escape to half guard, you need to immediately switch to technical stand-up or deep half entry. The athletes who win at the highest level are the ones who can chain three or four different escape sequences together without pausing. This isn't a position where you can think - you have to drill the sequences until they're automatic.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: The Jailbreak is all about turning defense into offense through constant movement and creative guard recovery options. In 10th Planet, we don't just escape to any guard - we're looking to recover to lockdown, to rubber guard positions, to electric chair setups. The traditional approach is too conservative, just trying to get back to closed guard. Instead, use the Jailbreak moment to enter into your attacking systems. When you create that space with your frame, you should already be thinking about which sweep or submission you're setting up from the guard you're about to recover. The best part is that your opponent is so focused on recapturing side control that they often don't see the deep half entry or the lockdown coming. This position is where you show that defense and offense are the same thing when you have the right mindset.

metadata.title: Jailbreak Top Position | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Jailbreak Top Position in BJJ. Complete guide covering control, passing opportunities, and counters. Specialized half guard top position with 65% pass success rate.

overview:
Jailbreak Top Position represents a critical transitional state in the half guard passing game, where the top player has successfully created significant space and established control while the bottom player attempts to recover guard. This position occurs when the bottom player extends their legs in a 'jailbreak' motion to create distance and prevent the pass, but the top player maintains connection and begins to work around or through this defensive frame. The position is characterized by the bottom player's extended legs creating a barrier while the top player establishes grips and weight distribution to neutralize this defense.

From a game theory perspective, Jailbreak Top Position represents a high-stakes moment where the top player must choose between multiple passing strategies based on the bottom player's leg configuration. The extended legs create opportunities for leg weave passes, smash passes, or backstep entries to the legs, but also present risks if the bottom player can quickly retract and re-establish guard. Success in this position requires reading the bottom player's intentions and maintaining forward pressure while preventing guard recovery. The position is particularly relevant in modern no-gi competition where dynamic guard retention has become increasingly sophisticated.
state_invariants: Top player maintains upper body connection with chest-to-chest pressure or heavy cross-face control, preventing bottom player from creating adequate defensive frames
Bottom player's legs are extended away from their torso in a 'jailbreak' configuration, with one or both legs attempting to create distance and block the pass
Top player's weight is distributed forward with hips driving toward the bottom player's center line, maintaining constant forward pressure despite the extended leg barrier
Bottom player is on their back or side with shoulders partially pinned to the mat, unable to fully turn away or establish seated guard position
Top player controls at least one grip on the bottom player's upper body (collar, underhook, overhook, or head control) to prevent escape to neutral standing position
prerequisites: Top player has passed beyond the initial half guard frames
Bottom player has extended legs to create distance in defensive jailbreak motion
Top player maintains forward pressure and upper body connection
Bottom player is unable to fully recover closed guard or seated guard
Top player has identified passing lane around or through extended legs
key_principles: Maintain constant forward pressure with hips driving toward bottom player's center line to prevent guard recovery
Control bottom player's upper body with heavy cross-face, underhook, or head control to limit mobility
Read bottom player's leg configuration and choose appropriate passing strategy (leg weave, smash, or backstep)
Keep weight distributed forward to prevent bottom player from creating enough space to re-guard
Establish grips that allow for quick transitions between multiple passing options based on bottom player's reactions
Prevent bottom player from turning to turtle or standing up by maintaining chest pressure and controlling far shoulder
Use leg positioning to block bottom player's hip movement while navigating around extended legs

counter_transitions.trigger: Bottom player attempts to create space by extending legs further
Bottom player keeps legs extended in static position
Bottom player retracts legs toward body to re-guard
Bottom player commits to half guard recovery with deep underhook
Bottom player attempts to turn to turtle position

decision_tree.condition: If bottom player's legs are extended and static with minimal hip movement
If bottom player is actively moving hips and creating angles with leg positioning
If bottom player commits to deep underhook or attempts to come up on elbow
If bottom player retracts legs quickly to recover closed guard or butterfly guard
If bottom player attempts to turn to turtle or go belly down

common_errors.error: Standing too upright and losing forward pressure while navigating extended legs
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player recovers full guard or creates enough space to stand up
common_errors.correction: Maintain low chest-to-chest connection with weight driving forward through hips, keeping shoulders above opponent's center line throughout the pass

common_errors.error: Attempting to pass without controlling bottom player's upper body first
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player uses frames and hip movement to re-establish guard or sweep
common_errors.correction: Establish heavy cross-face, underhook, or head control before committing to leg navigation, ensuring upper body is controlled throughout

common_errors.error: Committing to a single passing direction without reading bottom player's leg configuration
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player anticipates pass and easily blocks or counters with sweep
common_errors.correction: Read bottom player's leg positioning and remain flexible between multiple passing options (leg weave, smash, backstep) based on their reactions

common_errors.error: Allowing bottom player to create sufficient space to turn to turtle or stand up
common_errors.consequence: Position resets to neutral standing or turtle, losing passing advantage
common_errors.correction: Keep constant chest pressure and control far shoulder with underhook or cross-face to prevent bottom player from turning away or standing

common_errors.error: Overcommitting to leg entanglement attacks instead of completing the pass
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player uses time to recover guard or creates scramble situation
common_errors.correction: Prioritize completing the pass to side control or mount before considering leg attacks, unless clear submission opportunity presents itself

common_errors.error: Using only upper body strength to control position without proper hip placement
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player uses leg dexterity to recover guard despite upper body control
common_errors.correction: Drive hips forward and position them to block bottom player's hip movement while maintaining upper body connection

common_errors.error: Failing to adjust passing strategy when bottom player changes leg configuration
common_errors.consequence: Pass stalls and bottom player eventually recovers guard or sweeps
common_errors.correction: Continuously assess bottom player's leg positioning and switch between passing strategies (smash to leg weave, or leg weave to backstep) as their defense changes

training_drills.name: Jailbreak Pass Flow Drill
training_drills.description: Bottom player starts in jailbreak position with extended legs. Top player flows between three passing options (leg weave, smash pass, knee slice) based on bottom player's leg positioning. Bottom player provides moderate resistance and changes leg configuration every 10 seconds. Focus on reading leg positioning and maintaining forward pressure throughout transitions.

training_drills.name: Pressure Maintenance Drill
training_drills.description: Top player maintains jailbreak top position while bottom player attempts various guard recoveries (closed guard, butterfly, deep half). Top player focuses on keeping constant forward pressure and upper body control without attempting to pass. Bottom player gradually increases resistance level. Emphasizes weight distribution and connection over speed.

training_drills.name: Multi-Directional Passing Drill
training_drills.description: From jailbreak top position, top player must complete pass using specific technique called out by coach (leg weave, smash, backstep, etc.). Bottom player provides 50% resistance. Rotate through all major passing options. Develops muscle memory for each passing variation and decision-making speed.

training_drills.name: Jailbreak to Finish Positional Sparring
training_drills.description: Start from jailbreak top position. Top player wins by achieving side control or mount with three-second control. Bottom player wins by recovering full guard or sweeping. Reset after each success. Gradually increase resistance from 70% to 100% over multiple rounds.
training_drills.duration: 3 minutes per round, 5 rounds with increasing resistance

training_drills.name: Grip Fighting from Jailbreak Top
training_drills.description: Focus exclusively on grip fighting and upper body control from jailbreak top position. Top player works to establish dominant grips (cross-face, underhook, head control) while bottom player attempts to break grips and create frames. No passing attempts allowed. Develops grip hierarchy and understanding of control positions.
training_drills.duration: 2 minutes per round, 6 rounds alternating roles

expert_insights.danaher: The jailbreak top position represents a critical inflection point in the half guard passing sequence where the passer's ability to maintain forward pressure while reading leg configurations determines success or failure. The extended legs create a geometric puzzle that must be solved through proper weight distribution and strategic grip placement. The key mechanical principle is maintaining chest-to-chest connection while your hips drive forward into the bottom player's center line, creating what I call 'pressure through the legs rather than against them.' Many students make the error of trying to force their way through the extended legs with pure strength, when the solution is to use the opponent's leg extension as a guide for your passing direction. When the legs are extended, they become relatively static and predictable, allowing you to choose between three primary passing vectors: over the legs with a smash pass, through the legs with a leg weave, or around the legs with a backstep to leg entanglements. The decision of which vector to use must be based on the bottom player's hip positioning and defensive priorities. This position also teaches an important concept about passing in general: control the upper body first, solve the leg puzzle second. Without proper cross-face, underhook, or head control, even the most technically sound leg navigation will fail because the bottom player retains the mobility to re-guard.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, jailbreak top is where a lot of matches get decided because it's that moment right before you complete the pass where your opponent is making their last stand. I've passed hundreds of half guards in competition and the jailbreak is almost always the final defensive position they show me before I get to side control. The key thing I focus on is not giving them any time to think or adjust. The moment I feel their legs extend in that jailbreak motion, I'm already choosing my passing direction and committing to it with maximum pressure. In high-level competition, you can't hesitate here because guys like Lachlan Giles or Craig Jones will use that split second to recover deep half or hit a dogfight. My go-to from here is almost always the smash pass because it's the highest percentage and it puts maximum pressure on their guard retention. I'm driving my shoulder into their face, controlling their far hip with my hand, and just crushing through. If they try to turn away, I follow to their back. If they try to come up to dogfight, I sprawl and take the back step to their legs. The beautiful thing about jailbreak top is that every defensive option they choose opens up a clear passing lane if you're reading it correctly.
